title: AI System Design
blurb: The decision layer above individual AI techniques -- choosing between prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, and traditional ML, and combining them into a coherent, production-ready system.

intermediate: Designing retrieval into a larger architecture
advanced: Fallbacks when models produce bad output

description: Architecture-level decisions for production AI systems -- approach selection, hosted vs. self-hosted, caching, token budgets, failure handling, human-in-the-loop design, and scaling, combining what LLMs, RAG, Agents, and MLOps teach separately.

lessons.title: Choosing the right approach: prompting vs. RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. traditional ML
objectives: Apply concrete decision criteria to choose between the four major AI approaches for a given requirement
Explain how approach selection criteria changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect approach selection criteria with RAG vs. fine-tuning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Prompting alone fits when the model's existing knowledge and reasoning are sufficient and no current or proprietary facts are needed. RAG fits when the task needs current or proprietary information the model wasn't trained on, without needing to change the model's underlying behavior.
examples:
# decision criteria, not a preference ranking:
# needs CURRENT/proprietary facts, behavior otherwise fine -> RAG
# needs the model's BEHAVIOR itself changed, has labeled examples -> fine-tuning
# neither -> prompting alone is likely sufficient
# narrow, well-defined prediction task, latency/cost-critical, labeled data exists
# -> traditional ML may beat an LLM-based approach entirely
concepts: when traditional ML beats an LLM
commonMistakes: Defaulting to an LLM-based approach for every problem, including narrow prediction tasks a traditional ML classifier would handle faster and cheaper -- this is a genuine, common overreach.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact decision -- which approach fits a given requirement -- is one of the most frequently asked real AI system design interview questions.
lessons.explain: Prompting alone fits when the model's existing knowledge and reasoning are sufficient and no current or proprietary facts are needed. lessons.explanation: An end-to-end AI application typically includes: an input/request layer, a decision of which AI approach(es) to invoke, any retrieval or tool-use steps, the model call itself, output validation, caching, and observability -- each a genuine architectural decision point, not a fixed template.

lessons.title: Model and API selection
objectives: Choose an appropriate model/API based on task requirements, not just capability leaderboards
Explain how model selection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model selection with capability vs. cost/latency trade-off and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Model selection isn't simply 'pick the most capable model' -- it's matching a model's capability, latency, cost, and context window to the SPECIFIC task's actual requirements. A simple classification or extraction task rarely needs the most expensive, highest-capability model available; a complex, ambiguous reasoning task might need it.
examples:
# matching model choice to the ACTUAL task, not defaulting to 'the best model':
# simple field extraction from a structured document -> a smaller, cheaper,
# faster model is very likely sufficient
# open-ended multi-step reasoning over ambiguous input -> may genuinely need
# the strongest available model
# a real system might use BOTH, for different sub-tasks within the same request
commonMistakes: Defaulting to the single most capable (and most expensive) available model for every part of a system -- matching model choice to each sub-task's actual difficulty is a genuine cost and.
lessons.careerRelevance: This mixed-model pattern (cheap model for easy sub-tasks, strong model reserved for hard ones) is increasingly standard practice in real, cost-conscious AI system design.

lessons.title: Hosted API vs. self-hosted models — the real trade-offs
objectives: Weigh data sensitivity, volume, operational capability, and latency together to make a hosted-vs-self-hosted decision
Explain how hosted API changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hosted API with self-hosted/open models and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: A hosted API (calling a provider's model over the network) is simpler to start with and requires no ML infrastructure expertise, but means your data leaves your infrastructure and you're subject to the provider's availability and pricing.

# low volume + no dedicated MLOps team -> pushes toward hosted, even with
# sensitive-adjacent data, since operational risk of self-hosting badly can be worse
# very high sustained volume + existing MLOps capability -> self-hosted can
# become genuinely more cost-effective over time

lessons.title: Synchronous vs. asynchronous AI workflows
objectives: Decide when an AI workflow should block the user's request versus run in the background
Explain how synchronous AI workflow changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect synchronous AI workflow with asynchronous AI workflow and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A synchronous AI workflow blocks the user's request until the model responds -- simple to reason about, but the user waits for the full latency of every step (retrieval, model call, validation).
examples:
# the deciding question: does the user need to wait for THIS, right now?
# a chat response the user is actively waiting to read -> synchronous
# a multi-step agent task researching and drafting a report over 2 minutes
# -> asynchronous; block and make someone stare at a spinner for 2 minutes
# is a worse experience than 'we'll notify you when it's ready'
commonMistakes: Defaulting to synchronous request/response for every AI feature regardless of how long the underlying pipeline actually takes -- a multi-step or slow pipeline forced into a synchronous.
lessons.careerRelevance: This sync/async decision is a common, concrete AI system design interview question specifically because it reveals whether a candidate is thinking about the full pipeline's actual latency, not just the model call.
lessons.explain: A synchronous AI workflow blocks the user's request until the model responds -- simple to reason about, but the user waits for the full latency of every step (retrieval, model call, validation).

lessons.title: Caching AI outputs safely
objectives: Design AI output caching that accounts for staleness and personalization risk, not just repeated-query efficiency
Explain how AI output caching changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect AI output caching with staleness risk and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Caching an AI system's output for a repeated query can meaningfully cut cost and latency -- but AI output caching carries risks general caching (already covered in System Design) doesn't fully address: a cached response can become stale if underlying facts changed since it was generated (especially relevant for RAG-backed answers).
examples:
# two risks general caching (System Design's own topic) doesn't fully cover:
# staleness: a cached RAG answer about 'our current return policy' served after
# the policy changed -- the cache doesn't know the underlying facts moved
# personalization leakage: caching by raw query text alone can serve one user's
# personalized response to a different user asking the same literal question
commonMistakes: Caching an AI response keyed only on the raw query text, without accounting for personalization or fact staleness -- this can leak one user's personalized response to another, or serve.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is a genuinely common, costly mistake in real production AI systems -- a naive caching layer added purely for cost savings, without considering these AI-specific risks.
lessons.explain: Caching an AI system's output for a repeated query can meaningfully cut cost and latency -- but AI output caching carries risks general caching (already covered in System Design) doesn't fully address: a cached response can become stale if underlying facts changed since it was generated (especially relevant for RAG-backed answers).

objectives: Decide where and how retrieval fits within a larger system, treating it as one architectural component among several
Explain how retrieval placement changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: This lesson treats retrieval as an architectural decision, not a technique to re-explain -- the RAG course already covers chunking, embeddings, and reranking in depth.

# architectural questions RAG's own course doesn't focus on:
# WHEN does retrieval happen -- always, or only when the model signals it needs
# more information (connecting this decision to whether the system is agentic)?
# WHAT happens on empty retrieval -- proceed silently with no context (risking
# a confident wrong answer) or explicitly surface 'I don't have information on this'?
commonMistakes: Letting a system silently proceed with a model call when retrieval found nothing relevant -- this risks a confidently wrong answer; an explicit 'I don't have information on this' is often.

lessons.title: Context-window and token-budget design
objectives: Design an explicit allocation strategy for a fixed token budget across competing inputs
Explain how token budget allocation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect token budget allocation with truncation priority and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A model's context window is a fixed, finite budget that must be shared across the system prompt, conversation history, any retrieved context, and the user's actual query -- and LLMs' own course covers what a context window IS; this lesson covers how to ARCHITECT around its limit.
examples:
# an explicit allocation strategy, decided in advance, not discovered in production:
# fixed budget: 4000 tokens total
# system prompt: reserved, protected (e.g. 200 tokens, never truncated)
# user's current query: reserved, protected (e.g. 100 tokens)
# remaining ~3700 split between conversation history and retrieved context --
# WHICH gets truncated first when both together don't fit needs an explicit answer
commonMistakes: Not deciding a truncation strategy until a real production request first exceeds the context window -- this should be an explicit, tested design decision made in advance, not discovered as a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Token-budget design is a concrete, practical skill directly tested in AI system design interviews, distinct from simply knowing what a context window is.

lessons.title: Handling AI provider failures: rate limits, retries, and graceful degradation
objectives: Design handling for third-party AI provider rate limits and failures, distinct from general API rate limiting
Explain how third-party rate limiting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect third-party rate limiting with graceful degradation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Calling a third-party AI provider introduces a genuinely different rate-limiting problem than the general API rate limiting the APIs course covers: you don't control the provider's limits, they can change without notice, and a burst of legitimate user traffic can hit them unpredictably.
examples:
# why THIRD-PARTY AI rate limits are a different problem than your own API's:
# your own API's rate limiting (APIs course): YOU set and control the limits
# a third-party AI provider's rate limiting: THEY set the limits, can change
# them without notice, and your own legitimate traffic burst can trigger it
# unpredictably -- requiring a fallback plan you control, since the limit itself isn't yours to adjust
commonMistakes: Assuming a third-party AI provider's rate limits behave like your own API's, under your control -- they don't, and a real system needs a genuine fallback plan for when they're hit, not just.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction (your API's limits vs. a third party's) is a common, concrete point that separates a system-design answer that's actually thought through provider dependency from one that hasn't.
lessons.explain: Calling a third-party AI provider introduces a genuinely different rate-limiting problem than the general API rate limiting the APIs course covers: you don't control the provider's limits, they can change without notice, and a burst of legitimate user traffic can hit them unpredictably.

lessons.title: Fallbacks when models produce bad or missing output
objectives: Design specific fallbacks for AI-specific failure modes, distinct from general service failure handling
Explain how malformed output fallback changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect malformed output fallback with silent quality degradation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: AI systems fail in ways general service failure handling (Distributed Systems' circuit breakers and retries) doesn't fully anticipate: a model can return malformed output (breaking a strict downstream parser), or -- more dangerously -- can return confidently wrong or degraded-quality output with NO error signal at all, since nothing crashed.
examples:
# why a generic circuit breaker doesn't catch this AI-specific failure mode:
# circuit breaker: reacts to ERRORS and TIMEOUTS -- a clear, detectable signal
# silent quality degradation: the model call SUCCEEDS, returns a normal-looking
# response, but the CONTENT is subtly wrong -- nothing crashed, nothing timed out,
# so a generic circuit breaker has no signal to react to at all
commonMistakes: Assuming general circuit-breaker/retry patterns (Distributed Systems' own coverage) fully handle AI failure modes -- silent quality degradation specifically produces no error or timeout.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is exactly the kind of AI-specific failure mode that distinguishes a system-design answer built on real production AI experience from one that only knows general distributed-systems patterns.
lessons.explain: AI systems fail in ways general service failure handling (Distributed Systems' circuit breakers and retries) doesn't fully anticipate: a model can return malformed output (breaking a strict downstream parser), or -- more dangerously -- can return confidently wrong or degraded-quality output with NO error signal at all, since nothing crashed.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-loop architecture
objectives: Decide when full automation, human review before action, or human review only on low-confidence output is appropriate
Explain how human-in-the-loop changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect human-in-the-loop with stakes and reversibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Human-in-the-loop architecture means deciding where, if anywhere, a human should review or approve an AI system's output before it takes effect.
examples:
# the decision depends on STAKES and REVERSIBILITY together, not automation for its own sake:
# high stakes + irreversible (e.g. an automated financial transaction) -> mandatory
# human review before action, regardless of how confident the model is
# low stakes + reversible (e.g. a draft suggestion the user can freely edit)
# -> full automation is likely fine
# middle ground -> route only LOW-CONFIDENCE outputs to human review
commonMistakes: Defaulting to either extreme -- full automation regardless of stakes, or requiring human review for everything regardless of how low-stakes and reversible the action is -- both waste the.
lessons.careerRelevance: Designing an appropriate human-in-the-loop boundary is frequently the single most consequential architecture decision in a real, high-stakes production AI system.
lessons.explain: Human-in-the-loop architecture means deciding where, if anywhere, a human should review or approve an AI system's output before it takes effect.

lessons.explanation: MLOps already covers evaluation GATES -- the automated check a candidate model must pass before deployment.

lessons.title: Scaling AI workloads
objectives: Explain the batching and queueing economics specific to expensive AI inference, distinct from general System Design scaling
Explain how batching economics changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect batching economics with queueing under load and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: General System Design's scaling lessons (load balancing, auto-scaling) apply, but AI inference has its own specific economics: requests are often batched together before being sent to a model (since batched inference is typically more cost-efficient per-request), but batching means waiting for a batch to fill, adding latency.
examples:
# the SPECIFIC trade-off AI inference scaling introduces, beyond general scaling:
# larger batch size: more cost-efficient per request, but each request waits
# longer for its batch to fill before being processed at all
# when demand exceeds current capacity: add instances (cost), accept a growing
# queue (latency), or shed load (some requests explicitly degraded/rejected) --
# an explicit choice, not something to discover only when it happens live
commonMistakes: Assuming general auto-scaling (adding instances when load increases) is sufficient without considering batching's latency trade-off specifically -- AI inference's batching economics add a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reasoning explicitly about batching, queueing, and load-shedding trade-offs specifically for AI inference is a genuine, distinguishing depth in real AI system design interviews.

lessons.title: Privacy, security boundaries and observability at the architecture level
objectives: Name AI-specific privacy/security boundaries a general security review might miss, and synthesize the course's architectural mindset
Explain how prompt injection (boundary-level) changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt injection (boundary-level) with output/context leakage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: AI systems introduce privacy and security concerns a general web-security review (Cybersecurity's own coverage of injection, XSS, and OWASP) doesn't specifically address: user input can be crafted to manipulate a model's behavior (prompt injection, covered at the architecture-boundary level here, with full depth reserved for a future dedicated course).
examples:
# AI-specific boundaries a general security review focuses elsewhere:
# prompt injection: user input crafted to manipulate the model's behavior --
# a genuinely different attack surface than SQL injection or XSS
# output leakage: a retrieved document or training-data pattern inadvertently
# surfacing in a response to a user who shouldn't see that information
# -- both are architecture-level BOUNDARIES to design around here; full technique
# depth is reserved for a future dedicated Secure AI Applications course
commonMistakes: Assuming a general web-security review adequately covers an AI system -- prompt injection and context/output leakage are genuinely different attack surfaces a standard OWASP-style review.
lessons.careerRelevance: This closing synthesis is exactly the mindset real AI system design interviews and production incident reviews are testing for: treating every one of these decisions as part of one coherent architecture, not isolated technique choices.

exercises.title: Choose an approach: customer FAQ bot
exercises.prompt: A team wants a bot to answer customer questions using current, frequently-updated documentation. Which approach fits best, and why?
exercises.hint: RAG -- the task needs current, proprietary information the model wasn't trained on, without needing to change the model's underlying behavior

exercises.title: Choose an approach: brand voice rewriting
exercises.prompt: A team wants every generated response to consistently match a specific, unusual brand voice, and has thousands of labeled examples of that voice. Which approach fits best?
exercises.hint: fine-tuning -- this requires changing the model's actual behavior (tone/style), and there's enough labeled data to justify it

exercises.title: Choose an approach: spam classification
exercises.prompt: A team needs to classify millions of messages per day as spam or not, with strict latency requirements, and has years of labeled data. Should they use an LLM?
exercises.hint: likely not -- this is a narrow, well-defined prediction task with abundant labeled data and tight latency/cost constraints; traditional ML likely outperforms an LLM-based approach here

exercises.title: Choose hosted vs. self-hosted for sensitive data
exercises.prompt: A healthcare startup with no dedicated MLOps team needs to process sensitive patient data with an AI feature. Weigh hosted vs. self-hosted.
exercises.hint: genuinely conflicting factors -- high data sensitivity pushes toward self-hosted, but no MLOps team makes self-hosting operationally risky; a reasonable answer might be a hosted provider with strong data-processing agreements, or investing in MLOps capability first

exercises.title: Design a caching strategy for a repeated FAQ query
exercises.prompt: Design a caching strategy for a RAG-backed FAQ bot, addressing both staleness and personalization risk.
exercises.hint: key the cache on the query plus a document-version identifier (invalidating when source docs change) and ensure the cache key includes anything that made the response user-specific, or don't cache personalized responses at all

exercises.title: Diagnose a token-budget overflow
exercises.prompt: A chat system silently truncates the user's most recent message when conversation history is long, causing confusing responses. What's the design flaw, and the fix?
exercises.hint: the truncation strategy isn't protecting the user's current query; fix by explicitly reserving budget for the system prompt and current query first, truncating conversation history (or summarizing it) before ever touching the current message

exercises.title: Design a fallback chain for a provider outage
exercises.prompt: Design a fallback chain for a production feature when the primary AI provider is unavailable.
exercises.hint: e.g. retry with backoff, then fail over to a secondary provider if configured, then serve a cached or simpler deterministic response, then explicitly inform the user the feature is temporarily degraded -- never silently fail with no response

exercises.title: Choose sync or async: a report-generation agent
exercises.prompt: An agent researches and drafts a multi-page report over roughly 2 minutes. Should this be synchronous or asynchronous?
exercises.hint: asynchronous -- a 2-minute synchronous wait is a poor user experience; accept the request, notify the user when the report is ready

exercises.title: Choose sync or async: a live chat response
exercises.prompt: A user is actively typing in a chat interface and expects a response to appear. Should this be synchronous or asynchronous?
exercises.hint: synchronous -- the user is actively waiting for this specific response before continuing the conversation

exercises.title: Design a human-in-the-loop checkpoint
exercises.prompt: An AI system automatically approves or denies refund requests. Design an appropriate human-in-the-loop checkpoint.
exercises.hint: given real financial stakes, route low-confidence decisions and any denial above a certain amount to human review; low-value, high-confidence approvals could be automated

exercises.title: Diagnose silent quality degradation
exercises.prompt: A summarization feature has zero errors or timeouts reported, but users complain the summaries have gotten noticeably worse over the past week. What's likely happening, and what should have caught it?
exercises.hint: likely silent quality degradation (e.g. a prompt or upstream data change), which a generic circuit breaker wouldn't catch since nothing errored or timed out; a continuous evaluation/quality-sampling layer specifically watching output quality would have caught this

exercises.title: Design evaluation for a live system
exercises.prompt: Beyond a one-time deployment evaluation gate, what would you continuously evaluate in a live production AI feature?
exercises.hint: e.g. sampled output quality checks, user feedback signals (thumbs up/down, edits, abandonment), and monitoring whether the distribution of incoming requests has drifted from what the system was originally designed for

exercises.title: Design retrieval placement
exercises.prompt: Should retrieval happen on every request, or only when the model signals it needs more information? Discuss the trade-off for a general-purpose assistant.
exercises.hint: always-on retrieval is simpler and more predictable but adds latency/cost to every request even when unnecessary; on-demand (agentic) retrieval is more efficient but adds complexity and a dependency on the model correctly recognizing when it needs more information

exercises.title: Handle empty retrieval results
exercises.prompt: A RAG system finds no relevant documents for a user's question. What should the architecture do, and what's the risk of doing nothing special?
exercises.hint: explicitly surface that no relevant information was found rather than silently proceeding with a model call; the risk of silent proceeding is a confidently wrong answer with no grounding

exercises.title: Distinguish AI-specific rate limiting from general API rate limiting
exercises.prompt: Explain why handling a third-party AI provider's rate limits is a different problem than handling rate limits on your own API.
exercises.hint: you control your own API's limits and can plan around them; a third-party provider sets and can change their limits without your control, and your own legitimate traffic bursts can trigger them unpredictably, requiring a fallback plan rather than just adjusting a limit you don't own

exercises.title: Design for AI inference batching trade-offs
exercises.prompt: A team increases their inference batch size to cut cost, and users start noticing higher response latency. Explain what happened and the trade-off involved.
exercises.hint: larger batches are more cost-efficient per request but require waiting longer for a batch to fill before processing begins, directly trading latency for cost efficiency

exercises.title: Decide between adding instances, queueing, or shedding load
exercises.prompt: An AI feature's incoming request volume has grown past what current instances can handle. What are the architectural options, and how would you choose among them?
exercises.hint: add more instances (costs money but preserves latency), accept a growing queue (cheaper but increases wait time), or shed load by rejecting/degrading some requests (protects the system but explicitly sacrifices some requests) -- the right choice depends on cost tolerance and how bad a slow or degraded response is for this specific feature

exercises.title: Identify an AI-specific security boundary
exercises.prompt: Name a security concern specific to AI systems that a standard OWASP-style web security review wouldn't specifically address.
exercises.hint: e.g. prompt injection (user input crafted to manipulate the model's behavior) or output/context leakage (retrieved or training data inadvertently surfacing to a user who shouldn't see it) -- neither is a standard web vulnerability category like SQL injection or XSS

quiz.q: What primarily distinguishes RAG from fine-tuning as an architectural choice?
options: They are interchangeable in every case
RAG adds current/proprietary information without changing model behavior; fine-tuning changes the model's actual behavior and needs labeled examples
RAG is always cheaper regardless of scenario
Fine-tuning never requires labeled data

quiz.q: When might traditional (non-LLM) ML outperform an LLM-based approach?
options: Never, LLMs are always superior
For narrow, well-defined prediction tasks with abundant labeled data and tight latency/cost constraints
Only when no labeled data exists
Only for creative writing tasks

quiz.q: What's the main risk of defaulting to a hosted API without considering data sensitivity?
options: No real risk exists
Sensitive data leaves your infrastructure and is subject to a third party's handling and availability
Hosted APIs are always more expensive
Hosted APIs cannot handle any real traffic volume

quiz.q: What operational requirement does self-hosting a model introduce that a hosted API avoids?
options: None, they're operationally identical
Real MLOps capability and infrastructure investment to run and maintain the model reliably
Self-hosting requires no infrastructure at all
Self-hosting is always simpler to set up

quiz.q: What's the deciding question for choosing synchronous vs. asynchronous AI workflows?
options: Whether the model is expensive
Whether the user genuinely needs to wait for this specific response before doing anything else
Whether the system uses RAG
Synchronous is always correct for chat interfaces

quiz.q: Why might a long-running multi-step agent workflow be a poor fit for a synchronous design?
options: Agents cannot run synchronously at all
Forcing the user to wait through the full pipeline's latency (potentially minutes) is often a worse experience than asynchronous notification
Synchronous workflows are always faster
Agents only work asynchronously by definition

quiz.q: What AI-specific risk does caching an AI response introduce beyond general caching concerns?
options: No additional risk beyond general caching
Staleness (facts may have changed) and personalization leakage (a personalized response served to the wrong user)
AI responses cannot be cached at all
Caching always improves AI output quality

quiz.q: Why is caching by raw query text alone potentially unsafe for AI outputs?
options: It's always perfectly safe
If the response was personalized to one user's context, caching by query text alone can leak it to a different user asking the same literal question
Raw query text is never a valid cache key
Caching always requires a database

quiz.q: Why does token-budget design require an explicit truncation strategy?
options: Context windows are always large enough for any use case
Without an explicit strategy, a real request can exceed the budget in production with undefined, undesirable truncation behavior
Truncation strategies are only needed for fine-tuned models
Token budgets are fixed and never need management

quiz.q: What should typically be protected (never truncated) in a token-budget strategy?
options: Nothing should ever be protected
The system prompt and the user's current query, with conversation history or retrieved context truncated first
Only the retrieved context should be protected
Conversation history should always be protected first

quiz.q: Why is a third-party AI provider's rate limiting a different problem than your own API's rate limiting?
options: They are functionally identical problems
You don't control the provider's limits, they can change without notice, and your own traffic bursts can trigger them unpredictably
Third-party rate limits never actually apply in practice
Your own API never needs rate limiting

quiz.q: What does graceful degradation mean when an AI provider is unavailable?
options: The request should simply fail with no response
Having a real fallback plan -- queuing, a secondary provider, a cached response, or an explicit degraded-service message -- rather than silent failure
Degradation means the feature should be permanently disabled
Graceful degradation only applies to database failures

quiz.q: Why can't a generic circuit breaker catch silent AI quality degradation?
options: Circuit breakers can always catch this
A circuit breaker reacts to errors and timeouts; a model that returns successfully with subtly wrong content produces neither signal
Silent quality degradation never actually happens
Circuit breakers are only used for AI systems

quiz.q: What determines whether a human-in-the-loop checkpoint is warranted?
options: Always require a human, regardless of the situation
The stakes of a wrong output and whether the resulting action is reversible
Human review is never necessary if the model is confident
Automation should always be preferred regardless of risk

quiz.q: How does designing evaluation into a live system differ from MLOps's deployment evaluation gates?
options: They are the same concept
Continuous evaluation monitors live production behavior and request-distribution drift ongoing, not just a one-time pre-deployment check
Evaluation gates make ongoing evaluation unnecessary
Live evaluation only matters for fine-tuned models

quiz.q: What risk does relying only on a deployment-time evaluation gate leave unaddressed?
options: No risk is left unaddressed
The live system's behavior or the kinds of incoming requests can silently drift from what the original gate was designed to catch
Deployment gates catch every possible future issue
This only matters for non-LLM systems

quiz.q: What specific economic trade-off does batching introduce for AI inference?
options: Batching has no real trade-off
Larger batches are typically more cost-efficient per request but require waiting longer for a batch to fill, adding latency
Batching only affects error rates, not cost or latency
Smaller batches are always more expensive

quiz.q: When incoming AI request volume exceeds current capacity, what are the architectural options?
options: Only one option exists: crash the service
Add instances (cost), accept a growing queue (latency), or shed load (explicitly degrade/reject some requests)
Always shed load regardless of cost tolerance
Queueing is never an acceptable option

quiz.q: What is prompt injection, at the architectural-boundary level?
options: A database vulnerability unrelated to AI
User input crafted to manipulate a model's behavior -- a different attack surface than standard web vulnerabilities like SQL injection or XSS
A synonym for SQL injection
A technique only relevant to fine-tuning

quiz.q: Why doesn't a standard OWASP-style security review fully cover an AI system?
options: OWASP reviews cover every possible AI risk already
AI-specific concerns like prompt injection and output/context leakage aren't standard web vulnerability categories a general review targets
AI systems have no security concerns at all
OWASP reviews only apply to mobile applications

projects.desc: Given a realistic product requirement, choose and justify prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, or traditional ML as the approach.

projects.title: Design a safe caching strategy for an AI feature
projects.desc: Design a caching approach for a real AI feature, explicitly addressing staleness risk and personalization leakage risk.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning for a given problem?
interviewPreparation.a: Match the decision to what the problem actually needs: RAG when current or proprietary facts are needed without changing model behavior; fine-tuning when the model's actual behavior needs to change and labeled examples exist; prompting alone when neither applies. For narrow, well-defined prediction tasks with abundant labeled data and tight latency/cost constraints, a traditional (non-LLM) ML model may outperform any LLM-based approach entirely.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you design a fallback strategy when a model API is unavailable?
interviewPreparation.a: Build a real fallback chain rather than letting the request simply fail: retry with backoff, fail over to a secondary provider if one is configured, serve a cached or simpler deterministic response, and if none of those apply, explicitly tell the user the feature is temporarily degraded rather than silently returning nothing.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you cache AI outputs safely?
interviewPreparation.a: Beyond general caching concerns, account for staleness (the underlying facts may have changed since the response was generated, especially for RAG-backed answers) and personalization leakage (a response generated for one user's specific context must not be served to a different user asking the same literal query) -- both require the cache key and invalidation strategy to reflect what actually made the response valid and specific.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you decide when a human should be in the loop?
interviewPreparation.a: Base it on stakes and reversibility together: high-stakes, irreversible actions generally warrant mandatory human review regardless of model confidence; low-stakes, reversible actions can often be fully automated; a middle ground routes only low-confidence outputs to human review while automating the rest.

interviewPreparation.q: How do you design evaluation into a production AI system, not just at training time?
interviewPreparation.a: A one-time deployment evaluation gate isn't sufficient on its own -- the live system also needs continuous evaluation: sampled output quality checks, user feedback signals, and monitoring for drift in the kinds of requests coming in, since production behavior and usage patterns can silently shift in ways a pre-deployment gate was never designed to catch.

capstone.title: Design a Complete Production AI System
capstone.description: Given a realistic product requirement, design a complete AI system architecture, making and justifying every major decision this course covers -- not following a fixed template, but reasoning through each trade-off for this specific requirement.
deliverables: Approach selection (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, or traditional ML), justified
End-to-end architecture diagram showing the components actually needed for this requirement
Model/API selection, including whether multiple models are used for different sub-tasks
Hosted vs. self-hosted decision, justified against data sensitivity, volume, and team capability
Caching strategy, addressing staleness and personalization risk
Retrieval placement decision (if applicable), including empty-retrieval handling
Token-budget allocation strategy with an explicit truncation priority
Provider failure and rate-limit handling plan
Fallback plan for malformed or degraded model output
Human-in-the-loop placement, justified by stakes and reversibility
Continuous evaluation plan for the live system
Scaling plan addressing batching, queueing, and load-shedding trade-offs
Privacy/security boundaries specific to this AI system
At least 3 explicit trade-off justifications, stating what was sacrificed and why
One deliberately simplified component, with justification
One realistic limitation of the overall design
capstone.portfolioTips: The explicit trade-off justifications are what separate a genuine system-design answer from a checklist -- naming what you sacrificed (and why that sacrifice was the right call for this specific requirement) is exactly the depth real AI system design interviews are testing for.
